name: The Outage Anxiety Economy
deck: Losing power used to be an inconvenience; now it feels like an emergency, and the companies that sell reliability have quietly turned that fear into a strategic asset they can reprice at will.
core_bet: The bet is that keeping the lights on is no longer a utility's promise but a product you buy — and that the anxiety around losing power will keep rising faster than the actual outage rate. Whoever controls backup generation, batteries, and the physical guts of a data center gets to charge whatever the fear will bear, splitting the market between deep-pocketed hyperscalers who pay for certainty and everyone else who gets managed outages.

mechanism: The trigger isn't that the grid fails more often on average — it's that failure now costs more. A blackout in 2010 meant a spoiled fridge and a quiet evening. A blackout in 2026 means your home office goes dark, your electric car can't charge, your CPAP machine stops, and your smart-home locks and thermostat go stupid. The consequence curve got steeper even where the outage curve stayed flat, and people pay to flatten the consequence.

That fear scales up into industry with a different vocabulary. For a hyperscaler, an outage isn't inconvenient — it's an architectural failure, so backup generation moves from 'fallback' to 'design requirement.' Generac now sells to two hyperscale operators under global supply agreements signed in 2026 and carries a $1.6B data-center backlog, even as its residential standby business softened. Management literally reframed the home generator as 'an insurance purchase, not a premium feature' — the language of anxiety made into a sales pitch.

The same grid stress feeds both ends of the pipe. Sunrun turned solar-plus-battery into a distributed power plant, hitting a record 74% storage attachment rate and 4.647 GWh of networked capacity. Utilities like Alliant race to wire up 3.4 GW of contracted data-center load, projecting a 60% jump in peak demand by 2031. And the contractors who physically build the resilience — EMCOR with a $17.14B backlog, Comfort Systems with $14.06B — book records because the data-center buildout is really a reliability buildout in concrete and copper.

The money mechanic is repricing. Reliability used to be bundled into your utility bill as an implicit promise. Now it's unbundled and sold as a discrete premium — a generator, a battery, a hyperscaler backup contract — and the premium accrues to the vendor, not the grid. The grid absorbs the cost of intermittency; the backup-maker captures the reliability margin.
why_now: Three pressures converged at once. Extreme weather — wildfires, Winter Storm Fern — keeps knocking out supply and dramatizing every outage. AI-driven load growth is straining grids faster than they can be upgraded, with utilities like Alliant staring at a 60% peak-load increase by 2031. And culturally, every lost hour is now framed as a productivity-and-safety emergency because so much of daily life runs on always-on power. The clearest signal is Generac's split screen in Q2 2026: a second hyperscaler supply agreement and a $1.6B data-center backlog stacked against a 2% residential decline. When the industrial side is booming on backup demand while consumers pull back, reliability has been formally repriced — from a household appliance into a strategic industrial asset.
who_pays: Residential buyers pay a steep upfront premium for a standby generator or a solar-plus-battery system — thousands of dollars to insure against a fear. And the household that can't afford it pays too, in a different currency: it stays fully grid-dependent and eats the outages the affluent house next door rode out on batteries. Meanwhile ordinary utility customers absorb the system-wide cost of a stressed, intermittent grid without ever capturing the reliability premium that flows to the generator vendors.
who_profits: Backup-generation makers (Generac) and residential storage operators (Sunrun) capture the household premium. Utilities with data-center siting advantages (Alliant, NextEra) lock in decades of regulated returns on the buildout. And the contractors who pour the concrete and run the mechanical systems — EMCOR ($17.14B backlog), Comfort Systems ($14.06B) — book record work turning reliability into physical infrastructure.
tension: The whole distributed-resilience model runs on enormous materials and labor inputs, and it distributes cost brutally unevenly — solar-backed comfort for affluent homeowners, managed outages for low-income neighborhoods. There's also a margin illusion: Generac's $71M pretax tariff refund flattered its Q2 2026 EBITDA guidance. When that tariff relief expires, the real cost structure gets tested against the ruthless pricing discipline of hyperscaler buyers who don't pay retail-fear prices.
surprising_part: The trend isn't powered by outages actually getting worse — on average they aren't. It's powered by the consequences of an outage feeling catastrophic, so the market grows on anxiety, not on failure statistics. And the same company selling you a home generator as 'insurance' is quietly making its real money on hyperscaler contracts, using your fear as the retail-priced half of a business whose growth is really industrial.
one_sentence: When keeping the lights on becomes a product instead of a promise, society sorts itself by who can afford to buy certainty — and the companies selling it get to price fear as an asset.
societal_stake: A society where power reliability is purchased rather than provided equally is a society stratifying by resilience: the rich get solar and batteries, everyone else gets managed outages. That's not a hypothetical — it's the literal split in Generac's own results, where hyperscalers and affluent homeowners buy their way out of grid stress while small businesses and low-income communities facing the identical stress cannot. When the next storm hits, the map of who still has power will look a lot like the map of who has money.

evidence.fact: Data-center backlog reached ~$1.6B (Q2 2026); secured a second hyperscaler global supply agreement on 2026-06-24; C&I external net sales rose 29% to $556M while residential fell 2% to $617M; residential standby reframed as 'an insurance purchase, not a premium feature'; ~$71M pretax tariff refund boosted margin and full-year EBITDA guidance

Storage attachment rate hit a record 74% (Q2 2026, up from 71% in Q4 2025); networked storage capacity reached 4.647 GWh; management positions the platform as a 'distributed power plant' protecting families from 'an increasingly unreliable grid'
Contracted data-center demand reached 3.4 GW (Q1 2026); expected load growth by 2031 remained ~60% above 2025 levels; $13.4B capital plan for 2026-2029

Renewable/storage backlog ~29.8 GW at end of 2025, adding a record 4 GW in Q1 2026; FPL regulatory capital employed growing from $72.9B toward $79.7B, creating regulated returns on transmission and reliability investment
Record backlog of $14.06B (Q2 2026, up from $11.94B at FY2025); organic revenue growth of 51% (Q1 2026); Q2 2026 revenue $3.27B, driven by data-center mechanical and HVAC work
Remaining performance obligations reached a record $17.14B (Q2 2026, up from $13.25B at FY2025); data-center construction contracts were the single biggest contributor to RPO growth
Renewal lease-rate increases accelerated to 25.4% cash in Q2 2026 (from 6.1% in Q4 2025), signaling scarce power capacity and power-adjacent positioning as the competitive moat
$26B of projected capital expenditures through fiscal 2030, with over 85% focused on safety and reliability — modernization-driven growth built almost entirely on the reliability premium
